html:
The start of Japanese emigration to Brazil, when the ship Kasato Maru landed 781 settlers at the port of Santos on 18 June 1908. Most went to work on coffee plantations in São Paulo state.

Brazil needed workers on its coffee farms after it abolished slavery in 1888, and migration from Italy had slowed. Japan, whose countryside was crowded and poor after the Meiji Restoration, encouraged people to go abroad. Many had already gone to Hawaii, but the United States was closing its doors to Japanese.

Life on the plantations was hard, and many settlers moved on to buy their own land, growing cotton, tea and vegetables. About 190,000 Japanese came before the Second World War. Today Brazil has the largest community of Japanese descent outside Japan, about two million people, centred on São Paulo. From the 1990s many of their grandchildren moved the other way, to work in Japanese factories.
